title: RCC RefCert: A Research Toolkit for Structure-Fair Quantum Circuit Complexity
description:
RCC RefCert is an open-source toolkit for studying quantum circuit complexity. Given the parameters of your preparation model, you can compute a rigorous lower bound on optimal quantum circuit complexity from final-state data. Use the target state's exact spectrum or projector counts collected under a prespecified measurement protocol.

You can build your own quantum models and compare preparation strategies. With a density matrix, you can study how complexity is distributed across the subsystems of a pure or mixed state. Share the model, inputs and results for independent verification.

The toolkit is based on Reference-Contingent Complexity (RCC), introduced by Liu, Tian and Wu in Structure-Fair Quantum Circuit Complexity: An Auditable Information-Theoretic Lower Bound.

Features of reference-contingent complexity

Structural fairness gives complexity comparisons a physical basis

Quantum circuit complexity depends on what the physical setting provides and which operations count toward preparation. For example, one device may supply a pure ancillary qubit, while another must reset a qubit to obtain one. RCC takes structural fairness as a physical postulate. The reference accounts for the structure already present, and the model counts the resources used to generate additional structure. This gives the two preparations a common basis for comparison.

Final-state data certify a lower bound on optimal complexity

Once the model and its cost rules are fixed, optimal quantum circuit complexity is the infimum of the costs of all circuits that prepare the target to the required accuracy. This global optimum is generally hard to compute. RCC turns final-state data into a lower-bound certificate that applies to every successful preparation. Other researchers can verify it without reconstructing the preparation history.

Research tasks

  • Build models and verify reference certificates. Define channels, control rules and a reference state. Compute program semidensities and check reference bounds.
  • Calculate a complexity lower bound. Use an exact target spectrum or counts from a fixed-projector measurement. The worked example traces a certificate from the model to the bound.
  • Compare preparation strategies. Compare candidate programs for the same target and tolerance. The cyclic-reset and algorithmic-cooling examples show when upper and lower bounds meet and when a gap remains.
  • Study complexity with window RCC. Use your density matrix to compare subsystems on a common reference and resource scale. Resolve local and correlation contributions or track complexity during preparation.
  • Share and reverify a calculation. Save the inputs and results in a bundle for another researcher to recompute independently.
  • Reproduce the paper's reference calculations. Run python -m rcc_refcert reproduce --check. Three MATCH results compare the reference expectations, data and report. The paper-to-code map links the cases to the equations.

Run and share a calculation

With Python 3.10 or newer, install version 0.3.0 and run the four-qubit reset task in a new working directory.

python -m pip install "rcc-refcert==0.3.0"
python -m rcc_refcert cost template cyclic-reset > task.json
python -m rcc_refcert cost analyze task.json --bundle task.rccbundle

At the default trace-distance tolerance of 1/10, the result is [5,5] atomic slots. The model rules out shorter programs, and a five-slot program reaches the target with halt included. Change epsilon in task.json to try another tolerance and choose a new bundle filename for the next run. Verify the saved calculation with the following command.

python -m rcc_refcert bundle verify task.rccbundle

Version 0.3.0 adds preparation-cost intervals and subsystem complexity profiles. Both workflows support independent recomputation from a saved bundle.

Interpreting the results

Exact diagonal-preserving models can bracket the optimal preparation cost between a rigorous lower bound and the cost of a successful program. For general matrix models, the numerical checks give each candidate's cost and trace distance from the target. Window RCC compares state-side complexity at a fixed reference and control bandwidth. A finite-accuracy lower bound on preparation cost also uses the model parameters and one-shot corrections. The scientific scope explains the quantities and their units.

Further reading

The RCC paper also relates these bounds to the complexity–volume and complexity–action conjectures in high-energy physics when the preparation task and resource conventions are aligned.
